actions.justification: Mandatory first step for a patient with COPD and worsening dyspnea. Assess work of breathing, breath sounds, use of accessory muscles, and air entry to evaluate severity of exacerbation and rule out pneumothorax.
Mandatory baseline vital sign assessment to characterize hemodynamic stability and degree of respiratory compromise in this COPD exacerbation.
Mandatory chest X-ray to evaluate for pneumothorax recurrence (given history), infiltrates suggesting pneumonia, hyperinflation, and other causes of worsening dyspnea.

MANDATORY action: ABG is essential in COPD exacerbation to assess oxygenation (PaO2), ventilation (PaCO2), and acid-base status. Required within 60-minute deadline to guide oxygen therapy and NIV decisions.
Mental status assessment is critical in COPD exacerbation to detect CO2 retention and hypercapnic encephalopathy, which would indicate need for urgent NIV or intubation.

NIV (non-invasive ventilation) is a key evidence-based intervention in COPD exacerbation with respiratory failure. Assessing eligibility now prepares for rapid NIV initiation if ABG confirms hypercapnia or acidosis.

Patient has known COPD and history of pneumothorax with worsening dyspnea. CT chest will better characterize the lung parenchyma, rule out recurrent pneumothorax, and identify other causes of dyspnea such as pneumonia or pulmonary embolism beyond what CXR provides.
While SpO2 is 98%, patient has COPD with worsening dyspnea. Controlled supplemental oxygen (targeting 88-92% in COPD) supports comfort and safety during the assessment phase.

Patient has COPD with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum production, consistent with an acute exacerbation. Short-acting bronchodilator (e.g., nebulized salbutamol/ipratropium) is a first-line treatment per GOLD COPD guidelines for acute exacerbations.
CBC is indicated to evaluate for infection (leukocytosis), anemia, or other hematologic abnormalities contributing to worsening dyspnea in this COPD patient with increased sputum production.
BMP provides electrolyte status, renal function, and glucose — important baseline labs in COPD exacerbation to guide safe medication use and identify metabolic contributors.

Given this patient's complex comorbidities (COPD and history of pneumothorax) with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum, early pulmonology consultation is appropriate for specialist guidance on management.
Patient with COPD presenting with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum production — procalcitonin helps differentiate bacterial from viral exacerbation, guiding antibiotic therapy decisions.
Increased sputum in COPD exacerbation warrants sputum culture to identify causative organism and guide targeted antibiotic therapy if bacterial infection is confirmed.
Obtain blood cultures prior to any antibiotic administration to identify potential bacteremia in this COPD exacerbation with infectious etiology.

Patient with COPD exacerbation presenting with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum. Systemic corticosteroids (e.g., prednisolone/methylprednisolone) are a cornerstone of COPD exacerbation management per GOLD guidelines, reducing treatment failure, length of stay, and improving lung function. This is appropriate given the clinical presentation and is the most relevant available treatment action for COPD exacerbation.

Increased sputum production in a COPD exacerbation is an Anthonisen criterion (purulent sputum/increased volume) suggesting bacterial involvement. Antibiotics are indicated per GOLD guidelines for moderate-to-severe COPD exacerbations with increased sputum. Sputum and blood cultures have already been ordered, supporting appropriate antibiotic stewardship sequence.

With comorbid COPD and pneumothorax history, ordering lactate helps assess for any occult hypoperfusion or impending respiratory failure, even though current SpO2 and vitals appear stable. This provides additional safety monitoring data during the assessment phase.

Patient with COPD and worsening dyspnea with SpO2 98% and stable vitals. Given the comorbidity profile and potential fluid overload component contributing to dyspnea, a diuretic may help reduce any volume-related component. The AHA heart failure guideline is the closest applicable guideline among available options, and diuresis is a reasonable consideration for dyspnea with potential fluid retention.

Patient with COPD exacerbation and worsening dyspnea has received bronchodilator, corticosteroids, and antibiotics. IV fluids can support hydration status, though use cautiously given comorbid history. This is an available optional action appropriate for supportive care while awaiting diagnostic results.

While current BP and MAP are within normal limits, given the comorbidities (COPD, pneumothorax) and pending lab results, having vasopressor support available is prudent. Currently MAP is 103 so this is precautionary monitoring-oriented action from the limited available options.

Multiple labs (CBC, BMP, ABG, lactate, procalcitonin, cultures) are pending. Reviewing results will guide further management, including antibiotic selection adjustment based on sputum culture and severity assessment based on ABG.

Multiple labs (CBC, BMP, ABG, lactate, procalcitonin, sputum/blood cultures) are pending. Reviewing results as they return will guide further management including antibiotic selection and need for NIV.
